articles.title: Thanksgiving dinner is likely to be served with a side of political disagreement
articles.author: Matthew W. Kreuter, Kahn Family Professor of Public Health, Washington University in St. Louis
paras: Every year as Thanksgiving approaches, news stories are written about how holiday gatherings bring together people who see the world very differently, sometimes leading to uncomfortable dinner conversations. The stories usually include advice about avoiding awkward moments and topics that are off-limits, and navigating heated conversations if they arise.

As experts in health communication and public health, we are keenly aware of how conversations with family members and close friends shape people’s decisions and actions and that sometimes the benefits of having difficult conversations outweigh the potential costs. We wondered how often difficult conversations actually take place at Thanksgiving meals and what the conversations are about.

Although studies have demonstrated that Thanksgiving meals involving people with diverse political viewpoints were shorter by 24 minutes than meals among people holding similar views, we found no estimates of how often these conversations occur.

Our survey of 354 adults from 17 states found that over half – 57% – will share a Thanksgiving meal this year with at least one person from outside their household who sees the world very differently than they do. In 4 out of 5 of these cases, the way their viewpoints differ is politics.

The survey participants were initially recruited to represent differing perspectives on health; they were not randomly selected to represent the general population. That means the survey’s findings may not be generalizable beyond the study sample.
Table talk: What do Americans expect this Thanksgiving?

From Nov. 7-9, 2026, we surveyed 354 adults from 17 states about their plans for this year’s Thanksgiving. Respondents were part of an ongoing health knowledge monitoring and response system. Their mean age was 47.1 years; three-quarters of them were women; and they were racially and ethnically diverse, with 44% white, 33% African American, 15% Hispanic ethnicity and 8% another race or ethnicity. About 1 in 10 were rural residents, and 43% had children under 18 living in their home.
The questions about Thanksgiving meals were sent to 430 people on Nov. 7; 354 completed a survey, which is an 82% response rate.
Of the 354 respondents, 80% expected to share a meal with family members or friends from outside their household during the upcoming Thanksgiving holiday.

Those planning to share a meal with others from outside their household were then asked, “Holiday meals sometimes bring together people from different generations, with different views, or different life experiences. Thinking about your upcoming Thanksgiving meal, will anyone be there who sees the world very differently than you do?”
Almost 71% of those planning to share a meal with others outside their household said yes.

Asked “What are those differences about?” by far the most common response was politics, at 81%, followed by religion at almost 58%, differing views about people such as their career choices or relationships at 54%, health at 53%; and half of the respondents said money. A few mentioned other differences such as “raising children” and “parenting” and “gender expression” and “LGBTQ.”

Asked if they think any of those differences will be expressed during the meal, almost 60% said yes. This was especially true for differences in politics. A large majority – 79% – of respondents said that differences in politics would be expressed during the meal. Fewer respondents – 40% or less – expected that differences in views about people, money, religion or health would be expressed.
Then our questions got to who is expected to disagree – and what respondents anticipate the disagreements will be about. These responses varied by race and ethnicity.

White respondents were more likely than African American or Hispanic respondents to say that others at their Thanksgiving meal will view politics differently from them. African American respondents were more likely than White or Hispanic respondents to say that others at their meal will view money matters differently and were more likely than Hispanics to say that others at their meal will view certain people differently.

In short, it’s highly common for those gathered around any Thanksgiving table this year to have different views on key matters, but the differences you’re most likely to hear about during mealtime conversation are political.

Science tells us that conflict resolution improves through dialogue by reducing stereotypes and changing attitudes that tend to divide people. Holiday meals could provide some clues about how Americans navigate conversations with those who hold different viewpoints from them on politics, religion, money and health.
As one panel member commented: “I don’t keep people around just because they agree with me on something. I don’t cut people away because we disagree about something.”
Tori De La Vega contributed to this story.

articles.title: US foreign policy leaders say America should take an active role in world affairs – but no consensus on whether Trump’s policies are working
articles.author: Joshua Busby, Professor of Public Affairs, The University of Texas at Austin
paras: In the wake of the U.S. midterms, Vice President JD Vance blamed the Iran war for the election result. Affordability, Vance pointed out, appeared to be central to voters’ choices, with foreign policy decisions such as the Iran war generating higher fuel prices and rates of inflation. Polling before the election confirmed voters’ concerns – nearly two-thirds of Americans disapproved of President Donald Trump’s foreign policy.
But do foreign policy experts share Americans’ concerns?

To answer that question, the University of Texas at Austin, in partnership with the the Chicago Council on Global Affairs, recently surveyed 449 U.S. foreign policy leaders from the executive branch, Congress, think tanks, interest groups, media and academia.

Their responses matter because as the United States struggles to end the Iran war and navigate the fallout of tariff policies, these experts will be tasked with finding solutions to those pressing problems. These foreign policy experts are also likely to be advising presidential candidates in the run-up to the 2028 elections.
Areas of consensus and disagreement
On some issues, there is a consensus.

We found strong bipartisan agreement on the need for the U.S. to take an active role in the world, the importance of supporting NATO, and the use of force to support European allies if they are attacked.

Ninety-three percent of experts want the United States to take an active part in the world. That includes 83% of Republican experts, 98% of Democrats and 90% of independents. More than 70% of Democrats and more than 80% of Republicans and independents among foreign policy experts we surveyed agree that military power has been very important to American influence in the world. And more than 90% of experts of all partisan stripes agree that economic power has been very important.
However, these points of agreement mask key differences.

On the Iran war, 98% of Democrats and 73% of independent experts say war was the wrong decision, while 58% of Republican leaders say it was correct. While experts of all stripes recognized that tariffs would raise costs for Americans, there were stronger splits on whether tariffs were good for the U.S. economy. One hundred percent of Democrats and 81% of independents say they were bad, while 53% of Republicans say they were good.
These answers largely rally around partisan identities, but responses to philosophical questions about how the U.S. should pursue its interests proved more varied.

The Trump administration has challenged the foundations of U.S. foreign policy through its America First agenda, which favors U.S. domestic and economic interests over international agreements and global alliances.
On tariffs, efforts to expand U.S. territory and the use of force, the Trump administration used coercion to achieve its ends, including with close allies.

The Biden administration used tariffs to counter China’s dominance in areas such as critical minerals and batteries. The Trump administration has applied tariffs to rivals such as China and traditional allies alike, including in Europe and Asia.
The Trump administration also expressed interest in territorial expansion through the acquisition of Greenland and even Canada as a possible 51st state.
Besides military operations to depose and capture the Venezuelan president and war with Iran, the Trump administration has struck boats in the Caribbean suspected of running drugs.

We asked foreign policy leaders to assess the sources of U.S. power and whether there are downsides to a coercive strategy of American dominance. Specifically, we asked them: “In order to achieve U.S. foreign policy goals internationally, do you think it is more important for the U.S. to be feared or admired around the world?”

Sixty-two percent of Republican leaders suggested it is more important to be feared, while 97% of Democrats said it’s more important to be admired. Independents were closer to Democrats, with 81% saying it’s better to be admired.

We also asked whether countries have options to oppose U.S. coercion: “The Trump administration has used coercion, tariffs, punitive sanctions, and threats against many other countries, including traditional allies,” we said. Then we asked, “Which of these best captures your view?”

The respondents had three options to choose from. Thirty-nine percent of Republican experts agreed that “Other countries largely have to accept what the U.S. dictates.” No Democrats and 11% of independents agreed with that sentiment.

Fifty-five percent of Democrats and 54% of independents chose the second option: “Other countries will accept what the U.S. dictates in the short run but will distance themselves from United States order in the longer run.” A large percentage of Republicans – 48% – agreed with that sentiment. This suggests a recognition by Republicans that coercive power alone may have its limits.
A further 44% of Democrats and 35% of independents chose option three, “Other countries have viable options in the short and long run to resist U.S. coercion,” compared to only 13% of Republicans.
These partisan gaps suggest some strong cleavages about the foundations of U.S. power in the world. They also raise questions about how best the U.S. can achieve its interests on the world stage.

A subsequent U.S. president may have to engage in more vigorous dialogue with the American public about the sources of U.S. influence and power. The Trump administration’s coercive turn has some adherents, but many leaders see major costs to that approach and may be open to a new approach to U.S. foreign policy.
Enough damage to the existing world order has been done by the Trump administration, we believe, that a return to establishment internationalism of old is not an option.
Our survey suggests a ripe moment for new ideas and wide-ranging conversation about the U.S. role in the world.

articles.title: Forms, phone calls and portals: The hidden work that keeps American institutions functioning burdens parents most
articles.author: Lauren Hall, Professor of Political Science and Associate Dean, Rochester Institute of Technology; Institute for Humane Studies
paras: As a working mom of three kids, I spend a lot of time parenting. I also spend a lot of time coordinating insurance, physician and school forms and remembering passwords to six different school and sports portals. None of that is really parenting, and it’s not paid work either, but it takes time away from both.

I’m also a political theorist who studies how institutional design affects people’s daily lives. What many people characterize as unavoidable aspects of modern life actually provide important lessons about how various institutions are set up and who does the work to keep them functional.

Most American families deal with multiple complex institutions every week: a personalized mix of health insurers and medical providers, schools, tax authorities, Social Security and benefits agencies, daycares and camps and other kid activities, and state and federal programs such as Medicaid or SNAP.

Each of these programs has its own logic, including specific rules, portals, databases, forms, deadlines and definitions. This variation creates subtle misalignments across programs that compound over time. The physician needs prior authorization from the insurer, but the insurer claims the doctor needs a specific form. Meanwhile, the school needs the doctor’s document, and a benefits office might need proof that another agency already has in its system.
The people working to align all these systems are parents, often people with the least time and cognitive availability to handle the burden.

Political scientists Pamela Herd and Donald Moynihan of the Better Government Lab call this load administrative burden; that burden includes learning all the rules, figuring out how to comply with them, and then handling all the rippling demands that each individual task creates.
These burdens are not natural or inevitable. Instead, they’re the result of the way people have designed our institutions. The good news is that it’s possible to do things differently.

Most institutions weren’t intentionally designed with the user experience in mind. Instead, they’re the result of piecemeal decisions over decades, often the result of a complex interplay of interest-group lobbying, political jockeying and public demands.

Employer-based health insurance resulted, in part, from fear of socialized medicine during World War II. Public schools grew out of local communities and then had layers of state and federal regulations piled on top. Bureaucracies at different levels and of different types rarely talk to each other or bother coordinating their rules and processes.

And most of these rules and processes aren’t usually nefarious in intent. Documentation can prevent fraud, eligibility rules help allocate scarce resources, regulations can protect patients, and institutions have a vested interest in protecting themselves from mistakes and liability.
But each operates in isolation. The cracks are visible only to the person who has to navigate these silos – and that’s often an overextended parent.

It might seem like everyone bears the same administrative burdens, but they don’t. Life administration hits some groups harder than others; women, people with disabilities and lower-income people all interact more frequently with these fragmented systems and are less able to absorb the costs of those interactions.

For a middle-class American on salary, an hour on hold is a nuisance. For a waitress working for tips, it’s lost earnings or even lost employment. For many Americans, the administrative burden of applying for and proving eligibility for benefits is dramatic; the people who need these programs the most struggle to access them.

This is what researchers call a regressive effect in public policy, meaning that the costs hit hardest for those who can least afford it. Many institutions are effectively means-tested in reverse: The most vulnerable pay the most in terms of time, energy and money.
How to align fragmented systems
While there is no easy fix with institutions as complex as healthcare, education or public benefits, there are some options.
One useful model is universal design: the idea that we should build our environments – in this case, institutions – for people of different abilities from the start.

On the institutional front, this would mean more flexible hours to accommodate a range of users; a combination of email, phone and platform access; automatic enrollment or renewal when eligibility is already known; various plain language rules; and agencies sharing information, with permission, and working together to resolve conflicts between policies and rules so families aren’t forced into the role of unpaid institutional coordinators. Much of this will require not just language rewrites but significant investment in new systems.

Michigan provides an example of reform working at scale. In 2018 the state consolidated benefit application forms across five programs, reducing length and complexity. The original combined application packet was an overwhelming 1,000 questions and over 64 pages long.

The streamlined application process, which could be completed in about 20 minutes, not only improved the process for those applying. It reduced errors, cut down worker processing time and saved caseworkers 200,000 hours per year, presumably saving tax dollars along the way. Reducing administrative burden across programs is one of the few policy reforms with almost no downside.

For now, many Americans are like fish swimming in polluted water. We know something’s wrong, but we can’t see the cause. The next time you’re stuck on hold trying to fix a paperwork error with one agency before you can submit additional paperwork to another, it’s worthwhile to remember that this experience isn’t an inevitability of modern life. It’s the result of design choices – or failure to make choices – that can be changed.
Lauren Hall is a Distinguished Fellow with the Institute for Humane Studies.

articles.title: Massive super PAC spending did not secure Republican victories in 2026, but it remains a pernicious influence – in both parties
articles.author: Robert Boatright, Professor of Political Science, Clark University; Institute for Humane Studies
paras: It was almost as if all the money didn’t matter.

Republican super PACs substantially outspent Democratic ones in the 2026 midterm elections – particularly in Texas, where Elon Musk spent an astounding US$224 million on behalf of Republican Ken Paxton’s Senate campaign.
Yet Republicans lost across the board – regardless of whether they had super PAC support.
Not only did they lose, but the swing toward Democrats was remarkably consistent across the entire country, regardless of how much money was spent or what the fundraising imbalance was.

So, do the 2026 election results mean that super PAC spending, which represents the single-largest category of campaign spending in competitive races, doesn’t matter as much as we thought? Do they mean that Americans should worry less about the effect of these super PACs on politics?
As a political scientist who studies campaign spending, I would say no. Here’s why.
The limited effects of super PACs in general elections

Super PACs are political committees that engage in political advocacy but do not donate money to candidates or directly coordinate their strategies with them. Because of this, there are no limits on what super PACs can spend or on the size of the contributions they can receive.

They have limited effects on general elections. In competitive general election races for the House and Senate, it is usually the case that both candidates have significant funding, so the incremental value of each dollar declines as spending increases.
In each election cycle, approximately 90% of voters vote for the same party they did in the previous election. Voters such as these are unlikely to be moved by super PAC advertising.

Most importantly, super PAC spending is less efficient than spending by candidates or parties. By law, candidates and parties receive the “lowest unit charge,” or LUC, from television networks – that is, they pay the lowest permissible rate for advertising in a particular time slot. Super PACs do not receive the LUC, and thus they can pay two or three times as much per advertisement.

In a broader sense, however, the fact that super PACs cannot legally coordinate with candidates means that they are not able to spend money as wisely as candidates do. Usually, candidates and parties have access to the top consultants, they are likely to have information about what worked in the last election in their state or district, and they often have targeting information about voters.

A super PAC could acquire these things, but it cannot acquire them from the candidates themselves. In addition, many super PACs are ephemeral – they are organized to advocate for one particular candidate or set of candidates, and they do not last more than a few months. As a consequence, they do not have the ability to learn from their past efforts.

This may have been a particular problem in Texas. The sheer volume of spending by Musk in such a short time frame meant that there was little infrastructure to support his spending – all his super PAC could do was buy a lot of relatively untargeted advertisements.
Yet despite their often crudely targeted efforts to help candidates, super PACs still are a pernicious influence in politics for four reasons.
1. Super PACs spend a tremendous amount of money

Nearly two-thirds of super PAC spending in 2026 can be traced to only 100 people. These 100 people have very narrow business interests, but few of them are as controversial as Musk. One reason Musk’s massive spending was not helpful was that Paxton’s opponent, James Talarico, made his criticism of Musk a part of his campaign. Most super PAC donors are not as likely to provoke the sort of backlash that may have blunted Musk’s effectiveness in Texas.

Without public pushback based on an awareness of a donor’s agenda, this spending can reorient campaigns to be about the idiosyncratic ideas of an unrepresentative group of billionaires. It makes campaigns about something other than what parties, candidates and voters want them to be about. Parties and candidates, in turn, must raise more money than before just to be heard.
2. Super PACs shape elections long before November

Super PACs play a major role in primary elections, where voters are choosing among candidates of the same party and cannot simply use a candidate’s party label to choose whom to vote for. Some of the most expensive elections in 2024 and 2026 were primary elections in safe districts where one party was overwhelmingly favored to win the general election.

In the 9th District of Illinois, for instance, super PACs spent $9.1 million in the Democratic primary in support of six candidates. Few voters in the 9th District knew how much had been spent, who the groups were, or even what issues motivated these groups until after the election.

Super PACs have also increased their spending in nonpartisan municipal elections, where there is little advertising or media coverage and therefore voters often have even less information about the candidates or their policies.
3. Super PACs can be a vehicle for nefarious schemes

During the 2026 midterm campaign, conservative super PACs in Ohio and Massachusetts sent out deliberately deceptive mailings highlighting obscure socialist candidates, aiming to siphon votes away from the Democrats these groups were really concerned about.

While politics can often be dirty and these mailings were not illegal, they enable the candidates these groups supported to claim they have nothing to do with them. A candidate, a party or an established interest group has a reputation to protect, and voters can hold them accountable for the quality of their campaigns. Super PACs do not have to worry about this because they do not appear on the ballot, and they do not have members or stockholders who can put pressure on them.
4. Super PAC spending can affect how legislators behave

Even legislators with very safe seats must constantly worry about whether one vote, or one statement, might cause someone to spend a large sum of money against them. Many legislators cast votes they know their constituents will dislike in order to avoid antagonizing groups that might spend against them in their primary.
It’s legal, if deplored, by the public
Most Americans want limits on super PAC spending.

Many Democratic candidates in 2026 called for campaign finance reforms. It is tempting to believe that the new Democratic majorities in Congress will do something to rein in super PACs. There are many obstacles to doing so, however.

For one, the Supreme Court is unlikely to change its views on the legality of independent spending. The justices have decreed it is speech, and they see no constitutional restraint on this kind of speech.

While voters support campaign finance reform, they rarely list it as their top priority. And although Republicans benefited more from super PAC spending in 2026 than Democrats, many Democratic candidates have been dependent on it as well. The Democrats’ comfortable majority may make it easier than before for Democrats to receive more super PAC support.
Although super PAC support did not propel Republicans to victory in 2026, the real danger of super PACs is that most politicians, regardless of party, have become dependent upon them.

articles.title: The Milburn report sets out a plan to improve the lives of young people who are Neet – experts respond
articles.author: Lisa Russell, Professor of Education and Employment, Manchester Metropolitan University
paras: Former Labour minister Alan Milburn has finally delivered his long-awaited report on the UK’s nearly 1 million young people who are not in education, employment or training (Neet). In it, he proposes guaranteed work or training opportunities for all 16 to 24-year-olds, but also outlines the need to shift the focus away from benefits. It will be up to the government to decide which ideas to take forward, but our panel of experts has assessed some of the key issues.
Changed landscape for Labour on welfare reform
Tony McNulty, teaching fellow and lecturer in British politics and public policy

Everything about the ongoing debate by government around the issue of welfare reform is different this time. Former prime minister Keir Starmer’s attempts to secure reform in July 2025 could not have been organised in a worse fashion. Talk of it being a “confidence issue” was always a nonsense, real or imagined.

The rebellion happened in the context of severe restrictions on the winter fuel payment, the government’s insistence that it was not going to scrap the two-child benefit limit and its own assessment that the benefit moves would push an estimated 250,000 people into poverty. Within months of the Labour government being elected, it looked as though it had forgotten the reason for its very existence.

Whatever the intention, these plans were seen to be bereft of any sense of Labour values. This time around, the world has changed. Crucially, the three key architects of the rejected policy (Starmer, his chancellor Rachel Reeves and his work and pensions secretary Liz Kendall) have all gone – banished to the back benches or off to find pastures new.

The winter fuel payment was revisited and this allowance is now means-tested. The two-child benefits limit has been scrapped. An anti-poverty strategy has been articulated. Labour now has in Andy Burnham what many of the former rebels will see as a Labour PM.

Crucially, the ground has been prepared and the pitch has been rolled – by the whips office, the cabinet and by Burnham. It now feels like the debate is on Labour terms, unlike last summer. It is no accident that there has been an ongoing, sometimes subterranean, debate focusing on what to do with nearly a million young people on benefits who could and perhaps should work.

Milburn’s focus has been on this young cohort first and foremost – and couched in terms of working with them to ensure a productive role and meeting their expectations and aspirations. A Labour debate in Labour language. A political strategy and a government that takes its backbenchers seriously. This is miles from where it was last year. Although success is not guaranteed, the government now has a fighting chance to secure reform on its own terms – and that matters.
New guarantees must be appropriate
Lisa Russell, professor of education and employment

Young people do not suddenly become Neet at 16. While Alan Milburn’s focus on opportunities rather than long-term benefit dependency is to be welcomed, work that my colleagues and I have done on Neets suggests this is something of a blunt instrument for such a complex picture.

Our findings suggest that simply guaranteeing young people work or a placement ignores any long-terms effects that they might experience as a result of years of living with unmet needs. These could include poor mental health, bullying, disrupted education or undiagnosed and unsupported special educational needs and disabilities (Send).

Our five-year study, Mapping interventions for Neet young people in England, shows that the quality of support matters. Milburn’s proposal guarantees eligible young people a fully funded, six-month job. But there is an important difference between providing meaningful opportunities and requiring young people to participate in something that does not meet their needs. If education, training or employment pathways are poorly matched to a young person’s circumstances, the risk is that they’re left feeling frustrated and disengaged. This will not improve outcomes for anyone.

The report includes proposals for a “youth allowance” to replace personal independence payments (Pip) for under-25s and the health element of universal credit. But lasting change requires more than welfare reform alone. Alongside employment support, there needs to be less rigidity and less focus on exam outcomes in secondary schools. There’s also a wider need for better mental health provision and stronger support for young people whose needs have too often gone unrecognised. An “opportunity guarantee” can only work if the opportunities themselves are genuinely inclusive and supportive.
Previous policy hasn’t helped young workers
Rachel Scarfe, lecturer in economics

There are many costs to employing a worker, beyond the headline hourly or annual wage. The increase in employers’ national insurance contributions last year for workers aged 21 or over was just one in a series of these rises. There were also increases in 2019 to the automatic enrolment pension contributions that employers have to make, and sick pay was improved in 2016 as part of the Employment Rights Act. These costs are all linked to wages, so when wages increase, the cost of national insurance, pensions and benefits such as sick pay increase as well.

This is exactly what happened when Labour lowered the age limit for the national living wage from 25 to 21 in 2024. Employers often attempt to pass on their extra costs to workers by paying them lower wages. If this isn’t possible (because of a rising minimum wage), they may instead reduce hiring. In some cases, they may choose not to employ a young worker at all.

By proposing to abolish employers’ national insurance contributions for workers aged under 25, and recommending that automatic pension enrolment should not be expanded further, Alan Milburn has recognised this issue. The proposed cut in national insurance contributions is targeted at employers in retail and hospitality. These sectors employ many young people, often on the minimum wage. As a result, the joint effects of a rising minimum wage and increases in other costs are greater than in other sectors. Young people’s job prospects may have suffered as a result.
Employers should resist AI
Fabian Stephany, lecturer in AI and work

There is an economic reason to believe that AI is negatively affecting the entry-level jobs that young people typically apply for. Ultimately, a fundamental change is required. Both young and old people should be advised to have a basic understanding of AI and integrating it into their workplace. Much like with the introduction of computers decades ago, it’s fair to expect that everybody will be required to work with AI to some extent.

However, many entry-level positions are defined by repetitive, standardised work – or commodity work – for example, writing emails and memos or preparing presentation slides. AI does these tasks easily, making it a short-term economic incentive for companies to replace their junior workers with AI, and contributing to the Neet issue. Similarly, with “AI-washing”, companies can let go of junior employees while using AI as a scapegoat.

However, from my point of view, the problem is much more far-reaching. Companies are cutting off their own talent pipeline by not investing in junior workers, as they will not have experts five or ten years down the road. This will have dramatic consequences, as experts are needed more, not less, when it comes to AI. Firms would see long-term gain if they invested in developing young people’s skills.

To escape this dilemma, the government should do everything it can to incentivise firms to focus on the human. Though it can cost employers when young people make mistakes while they’re learning, companies should instead speed up the process of building staff expertise in using AI.
Lisa Russell receives funding from the Leverhulme Trust.
Rachel Scarfe is a member of the Labour Party.
Tony McNulty is a member of the Labour Party.

articles.title: Could your personality be affecting how you feel about social media?
articles.author: Claire Hart, Associate Professor of Psychology, University of Southampton
paras: Social media offers everyone the same basic promise: post something about yourself and get responses from other people. Whether it’s a holiday, a promotion or just a midweek meal, these days many people’s lives are shared online.

But could it be that what users feel they get back from the exchange depends on their personality? Our research has found that people who are higher in a trait called “narcissistic admiration” tend to be more positive about their online interactions. Narcissistic admiration is when someone goes out of their way to attract attention and validation as a way of boosting their self-esteem.

At the same time, those higher in narcissistic rivalry (positioning themselves as superior to others) and narcissistic vulnerability (those struggling with insecurity) reported fewer favourable social outcomes.

We initially thought differences in how they presented themselves online might help to explain these differences. But when we followed people’s actual social media posts over three weeks, we found that wasn’t the case. Instead, our findings pointed towards another possibility. What people expect from social media, and whether they feel they get it, may be an important part of the story.

We often use the term “narcissistic” to describe someone who loves attention. But narcissistic traits exist on a continuum – we all have them to some degree. Psychologists also distinguish between narcissistic traits.

Narcissistic admiration involves wanting to stand out, impress others and gain admiration and status. Narcissistic rivalry is more antagonistic and involves maintaining superiority, partly by devaluing others.

Vulnerable narcissism looks different. People higher in this trait tend to have a more fragile sense of self and greater sensitivity to rejection and how they feel they are being judged by their peers.
What people really think of us

Social media is an interesting environment in which to study these traits. It offers opportunities to attract attention and admiration, but also frequent feedback about whether other people have responded as we hoped.

In our research, we examined more than 1,000 social media users across Brazil, Indonesia and the UK. Participants completed questionnaires measuring their levels of narcissistic admiration, rivalry and vulnerability, alongside questions about what they felt they gained from their social media interactions.

People higher in narcissistic admiration tended to feel they gained more from their social media interactions. This included factors such as greater levels of attention and validation, and more opportunities to initiate relationships.

Those higher in narcissistic rivalry and vulnerability reported less favourable experiences. They felt less close to others and that they received less attention. This raised an obvious question: why?

One possibility was that people with different narcissistic traits were simply presenting themselves differently online. So, in another paper we looked much more closely at what happened in people’s everyday social media lives.

We followed 154 adults over 21 days, repeatedly asking them about posts they had made. Participants told us what they expected to get from their posts and, later, what they felt they had received. We also asked about their wellbeing.

Some of the patterns we’d found previously appeared again. People higher in narcissistic admiration reported more favourable daily interpersonal outcomes. Those higher in rivalry reported poorer outcomes when it came to relationships – that is, initiating them, maintaining them and staying close to people. Vulnerable narcissism was associated with lower levels of closeness and less ability to maintain relationships.
But differences in how people presented themselves online didn’t explain this variation in perceived social outcomes. Instead, people’s expectations provided an intriguing clue.
People higher in vulnerable narcissism expected to be more popular and get more attention and validation from their social media posts than they subsequently felt they received.

Vulnerable narcissism was also consistently associated with lower wellbeing in this study. And when people expected a post to help manage their relationships but then felt that it hadn’t, this mismatch was more keenly felt among those with higher levels of vulnerable narcissism.

This doesn’t mean that unmet expectations caused poorer wellbeing. Nor did we objectively count every like, comment or message that our participants received. Our findings concern people’s perceptions of what they got back.
But it suggests that understanding people’s experiences of social media may require looking beyond what they post. Who we are and what we expect from other people may matter too.

So what can we do with this? Our findings don’t suggest that people should simply expect less from social media. Wanting connection, attention or reassurance from other people is a normal part of life.

But they do suggest that it may be useful to think about what we are expecting a post to achieve. Are we sharing something because we want to connect with others? Are we looking for reassurance or validation? Are we hoping that one particular person will respond?

If the response feels disappointing, it may be worth considering not only what came back, but also what we had hoped would happen. Becoming more aware of those expectations may help us to understand our own reactions to social media. Otherwise, we could assume that how we feel is simply a consequence of the response itself.

There is a broader lesson here too. Discussions about whether social media is “good” or “bad” for our wellbeing often focus on platforms, screen time or what people post. Our findings add another layer: the same online environment may be experienced very differently depending on the person using it and what they hope to get from it.

articles.title: Your First Home: government loan scheme for first-time buyers could strain an already punishing property market
articles.author: Corinna Elsenbroich, Reader in Computational Modelling, University of Glasgow
paras: Housing in the UK has become markedly less affordable over the last 25 years. Between 2000 and 2025, English house prices rose by about 250% in cash terms (roughly 85% in real terms), while median earnings only doubled in cash terms, and rose by around 10% in real terms.

The median English house price is now over seven times median full-time earnings, up from around four in 2000. The increasing disconnect between house prices and wage growth is hitting first-time buyers particularly hard.

Mortgage deposits present the biggest hurdle to getting on the property ladder. While deposits varied until the 2008 financial crisis, 20% deposits have been the norm since 2009 – now an insurmountable barrier for most first-time buyers.

To address this problem, the UK government keeps reaching for the same fix: equity loan schemes for first-time buyers. The first of these was the 2013-2023 Help to Buy scheme in England. The UK government announced its successor, Your First Home, in September 2026. It will be available from February 2027.

The goal of these schemes is noble, but supporting market entry in this way could potentially pour fuel onto an already overheating market. This was exactly what happened with Help to Buy, which offered first-time buyers a government loan of up to 20% of a new-build property’s price (40% in London from 2016). Buyers had to provide a 5% deposit.

The government’s evaluation report showed that the scheme supported over 387,000 purchases. It also stimulated housebuilding – around 15% of all new dwellings built in England from 2013 to 2023 are attributable to the scheme.

However, the report also finds that it contributed to higher house prices, as it raised the purchasing power of house buyers without substantially increasing the number of homes. Comparing prices in the Wales/England border region, prices were around 2% higher on the English side, where Help to Buy was introduced one year ahead of Wales.

Labour’s new Your First Home scheme was announced in September and ratified in the October budget, amid accusations that it will have the same effect. Ministers claim that Your First Home will avoid the pitfalls of its predecessor through income caps, targeting the scheme at those that cannot get some or all of the deposit from their parents (the “bank of mum and dad”).

Your First Home gives first-time buyers of new builds a 20% equity loan (40% in London), interest-free for the first five years, with regional price caps. Buyers only need a minimum deposit of 2.5%, cannot provide more than a 15% deposit, and there is a household income cap of £110,000 (or £140,000 in London).
Help to Buy included no income caps, and buyers needed a 5% deposit (with no upper cap). Despite these changes, Your First Home will likely have the same impact.

Our research has tested the effect of these changes to equity loans in a computational model of the English housing market. We found that there is no material difference in market effects between the two schemes: both lead to the same kinds of price increases for owner-occupier homes.

We tested some hypotheses in model experiments. We looked at whether house price inflation could be curbed through better targeting – either through the lower deposit requirement or different salary caps. We also tested the effects of restricting eligibility to new homes only.

We found that reducing the buyer deposit from 5% to 2.5% made no significant difference in house price outcomes: both stimulated the market equally. However, salary caps had the potential to curb house price inflation, but they had to be relatively low.

A salary cap of £50,000 (coupled with a house price cap at £300,000) had almost no inflationary effect, and each £10,000 increase lead to proportionate price rises. It made little difference to house price inflation whether access was restricted to new homes or any homes on the open market.

Interestingly, in our model, the new scheme did lead to lower local rents. With more renters able to access the mortgage market – a likely effect of the low 2.5% deposit requirement – demand for rental housing would decrease. In turn, landlords would lower rents or put homes up for sale, thus increasing the supply in the owner-occupier market.
The conclusion from our analysis is that there is no silver bullet for making housing more affordable, other than the long-term solution of building more homes to consistently increase supply.
If the government genuinely wants to increase access to housing without further pricing people out of the market, income caps have to be considered carefully.

Although Your First Home has an income cap, it is too high. It currently equates to the combined salaries of two people both earning near the top 10% of earners, and will not restrict access in any meaningful way.

Short-term fixes, involving either subsidies for some sectors or increased taxes (for example on expensive housing), are extremely difficult to design without also causing unintended effects – not just for those buying and selling houses, but also for those who rent, since the rental and the purchase markets are so closely intertwined.
The new scheme will undoubtedly allow some people to fulfil their dream of home ownership. But for many, it could exacerbate the housing crisis even further.

articles.title: What Scotland is getting wrong on recycling – and Wales is getting right
articles.author: Ian Williams, Professor of Applied Environmental Science, University of Southampton
paras: Scotland has ambitions to become an environmental leader, but its recycling rate has just fallen to a five-year low.

The Scottish household recycling rate fell from 44.3% in 2024 to 42.8% in 2025, according to recently released figures. These figures also show the levels vary widely across the country, with Glasgow one of the lowest local authorities at only 24% and Clackmannanshire at 56%. The Scottish government had previously set a recycling target of 70% of waste by 2025.

It is tempting to blame Scottish households. But research has shown recycling is shaped by social, cultural and structural conditions. Participation improves when services fit people’s everyday lives and make recycling convenient. People need authorities to provide suitable local infrastructure, services and behavioural support to enable effective recycling.

Scotland’s recycling services remain inconsistent and confusing. This is partly down to the continuing variation between local authority systems. Depending on where someone lives, there can be differences in which materials are accepted, container types and colours and whether glass is collected at the kerbside.
The wide variation between councils, from 18.2% to 56.5%, points to inconsistent services rather than individual attitudes alone.

Meanwhile, Scotland has struggled to introduce a return scheme for drinks containers, where a deposit is paid and then returned when recycled. Initially expected to start in October 2025, this has been postponed to October 2027, and will no longer include glass, due to wrangles with the UK government over devolved powers.
This was expected to raise recycling levels of eligible drinks containers to around 90%. A similar deposit scheme in Ireland has been very successful at pushing up recycling levels.

UK-wide figures also show a distinct difference between the four nations: Wales recycled 58.6% (up from 4.8% of household waste in 1998-99), Northern Ireland 50.1%, England 43.8% and Scotland comes bottom at 42.7% in 2024. These outcomes reflect political choices, not simply how diligently households sort their rubbish. Scotland’s lower rate reflects lack of access to convenient collection systems, cost barriers, limited reprocessing capacity and increasing incineration of recyclables.
Overall, recycling has stalled across England, Scotland and Northern Ireland while incineration of waste has expanded.
The municipal rate of recycling has increased to 68.4% in 2024-25. Municipal waste includes all local-authority-collected waste, including some commercial waste, street sweepings and litter bins.
But Wales shows that stagnation in recycling levels is not inevitable, and the nation has become a global leader on this front.

This reflects a sustained Welsh government policy, reinforced in 2021 with a new approach that set statutory local authority targets, invested in collections, as well as monitoring and political backing. Wales also imposed a moratorium on new large-scale energy-from-waste developments in 2021.

The Welsh system is not perfect. Its municipal rate remained below the 70% national target for 2024-25. Nevertheless, 20 of its 22 local authorities improved, demonstrating what sustained institutional pressure can achieve. Its experience suggests that targets work best when they are backed by infrastructure, accountability and stable long-term policy.
The first UK recycling in the early 2000s focused on relatively accessible materials such as paper, glass, metals and garden waste.
But further progress depends on addressing food waste, plastic films, textiles, electrical products and complex packaging.

These streams are harder to collect, separate and process, while markets for some recovered materials, where waste is reused, remain uncertain. Variable quality, volatile prices and weak demand for some materials increase costs and risk, potentially leaving councils without buyers.

Another reason recycling have not climbed as high as predicted is that people cannot recycle materials that councils do not collect. To help people recycle more it is important to eliminate confusing labels, redesign packaging that was never designed to be recycled or create new markets for recovered materials.

It’s important to note that landfill reduction is also an important environmental achievement, and in Scotland, for instance, landfill use has declined – down 82.5% since 2011 – although incineration has increased. In 2024 1.86 million tonnes was incinerated, an increase of 239,000 tonnes (14.7%) from 2023. Poorly managed landfill sites can pollute soil and water, release methane and require monitoring long after closure. The 1999 EU Landfill Directive, landfill tax, statutory targets and kerbside collections helped transform the system.

But the UK is increasingly burning what it no longer wants to bury. In 2024, 63 energy-from-waste plants burned 16.8 million tonnes of residual waste. Since 2024, there are ten incinerators under construction in England and two in Scotland, but none in Wales and Northern Ireland. As people recycle more there’s less need for these, so why are so many being built?

For non-recyclable waste, modern incineration may be preferable to landfill. It reduces waste volume and can generate electricity or heat. But it is controversial. Incineration is the dirtiest way the UK generates power. It emits carbon and causes smells as well as destroying materials that could otherwise remain in use. It also often causes nearby residents to worry about health risks.

In 2024, 82.3% of Scottish household waste classified as “other diversion from landfill” was managed through incineration. Landfilled household waste fell by 37.7%, but the quantity managed through “other diversion” rose by 16.1%. Scotland is therefore managing its residual waste differently, but without achieving an equivalent improvement in waste prevention or recovering or reusing materials.
The UK’s reduction in how much waste it deposits into landfill was the first waste revolution. The next change must be preventing waste and keeping products and materials in use for longer.

Governments should ensure residual waste contracts do not penalise councils for reducing rubbish. They should reward durable, repairable and genuinely recyclable products. Priority should be given to food, flexible plastics, textiles, electrical equipment and complex packaging.

Wales shows that sustained recycling progress is also possible. The next waste revolution will begin when conserving materials takes priority over finding another way to destroy them. Those in Scotland who want the country to take an environmental leadership role should take note.
Ian Williams receives funding from UK Research Councils, including the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC) and its Impact Acceleration Account.

articles.title: National ground stop response highlights critical errors in public reassurance – saying ‘nothing nefarious’ did the opposite of quelling public concern
articles.author: Shannon A. Bowen, Professor of Journalism and Mass Communications, University of South Carolina
paras: Thousands of travelers were stranded on Nov. 13, 2026, when the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all domestic flights in the U.S. because of what they said were failures in decades-old air traffic communications systems. Crisis communications expert Shannon A. Bowen, a scholar at the University of South Carolina’s College of Information and Communications, spoke with The Conversation’s Politics and Legal Affairs Editor, Naomi Schalit, about how the Trump administration handled the first day of the crisis.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
Is there a first principle in crisis communications?

The first principle would be to react quickly and react with accuracy, react with everything you know at the moment, truthfully, but always react quickly. Because if you delay until you gather information, a vacuum will ensue. Information fills that vacuum that may not be accurate. And so that’s the enemy of accurate crisis communication, but you want to always speak quickly and be the most authoritative and definitive source, even if very little information is known.
What did we see on the day of the ground stop?

A crisis unfolded and to the administration’s credit, they did react very quickly, in a way that offered the information that was known at the time, even though not a lot was known about why the ground stop was issued until later.
You’re speaking about the short press conference that afternoon with Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin?

He did keep saying that nothing nefarious was at hand. And for a crisis communication scholar, you would not want to introduce the idea that something nefarious was at hand, unless, indeed, something nefarious was at hand. So by the very act of introducing this concept and this idea, I think the talking point, “Nothing nefarious,” then went across multiple networks, and it became the center of a controversy rather than quelling a controversy.

By saying nothing nefarious is at hand, that indeed confirmed something nefarious was at hand, even if the nefariousness was only the mismanagement of the air traffic control systems routers that they claimed caused the problem. By introducing this idea, I believe it did bring to mind that there may be other state actors behind whatever happened, that it could be a cyber attack. It would have been better to say, “We have evidence that this was not a cyber attack but a hardware failure.”
How did the later press conference with Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy go from your perspective as an expert on crisis communications?
They handled the questions that they received correctly. They told us as much information as they knew.
However, they did seem to downplay the extent of this crisis, because we have to remember the traveling public is not just people trying to get to business meetings.

We had football teams stranded. Now football Saturday, all over the SEC, has been disrupted. And there’s probably disruption in other areas of the country, but to us in the South, SEC football is almost a religious experience on Saturday. Luckily, the University of South Carolina football team had already flown out. But our marching band was stuck in this crisis, and so we have a lot of ripple effects from something like this happening, and it definitely says to me that this was an emergency situation. It wasn’t simply a crisis, it was an actual emergency of impending disaster-level scale.

If it were simply routers being overloaded, as we’ve been told, why wouldn’t they already know this situation and restart those routers the night before or over Friday night after most of the traveling public is out of the air?
What was Mullin’s and Duffy’s job when they got out there? What did they need to do?

To inform the public about the danger, why this happened, the extent of the problem, and what they’re doing to remediate the problem. We keep hearing that they’re asking for US$30 billion and more to repair the whole infrastructure for the air traffic control system, which is great, but what are they doing right now?

How do we know that flights in the air, right this minute, are any safer than the ones yesterday, a minute before the ground stop? Do we have that information? I don’t feel confident that they addressed that question appropriately. I don’t think that the traveling public entirely feels safe at this point or adequately informed that they will arrive at their destination.
They introduced politics into the press conference as well, didn’t they?

It’s something that they have the prerogative to do. They are both political appointees and members of the cabinet. So I understand that aspect, but I really wish they had addressed the traveling public’s concerns more overtly before making it political, that they need more money to fix this. We know they need more money to fix it, and I’m sure the American taxpayers are aware of the problem and willing to fund those corrections. But the more expedient issues would be, what about all these people who were stuck in airports?
Were there warning signs for this crisis?

I believe there were. We had another ground stop about three years ago, due to air traffic control problems, and that is what we call in crisis communications a “prodrome,” a warning sign of larger impending problems. When you see these types of warning signs, it really gives us a reason to think it’s going to get worse.

Duffy did say on Nov. 13 that, because of the condition of the air traffic infrastructure, “you will have more” ground stoppages. If you had a piece of advice for the administration regarding their future communications, what would you tell them?

I would say to communicate in advance as much as possible, so if you’re even considering a ground stop, it may be a good idea to put out a public notice so that people don’t go to the airport on a vacation flight, maybe they delay that for a week or two. It might also be a good idea to speak with the airline industry representatives and say, “Here’s what we’re thinking. Can you work with us? How can we make this better for the traveling public?” Also, if 17 of 22 routers were malfunctioning, could we have had a partial ground stop at only the affected airports, rather than a nationwide stop?
My silly last question: Do crisis communications experts have any theories about Friday the 13th?

We consider it more of a superstition, but I have noticed that there does tend to be a lot of activity on Friday the 13th. It might be placebo effect, it might be because we expect something bad to happen and we’re looking for it. But that day does seem to always have some type of activity. This is also when organizations release bad news, oftentimes, they say, “Let’s hold it until Friday the 13th, because bad news is expected.” People will assume, on Friday the 13th, that negative things are going to come out, so the shock value won’t be as much.
Shannon A. Bowen received funding in 2022-2023 from The National Science Foundation as PI on a grant studying disaster management.

articles.title: Debate in New York City over city-run groceries is not just about food, but something bigger
articles.author: Nevin Cohen, Professor, Graduate School of Public Health and Health Policy, City University of New York
paras: New York City is moving closer to launching its effort to counter food inflation by opening five city-run grocery stores. Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced in May 2026 that the first store would open in the Hunts Point neighborhood of the South Bronx in 2027, with another in East Harlem to follow.

Five stores, one in each borough, are unlikely to substantially change grocery prices in a city with nearly 1,000 supermarkets and more than 8 million inhabitants. But each could make a meaningful difference to the grocery bills of local shoppers by selling essentials at below-market prices.

Even with just five planned stores set to open in lower-income neighborhoods, the initiative has ignited fierce opposition from independent grocers, supermarket trade associations and a coalition representing immigrant-owned food businesses.
What explains this pushback?

As a food policy scholar, I believe this opposition is about more than the immediate economic impact of five stores. It is about the precedent they could establish. Mamdani’s initiative challenges an entrenched expectation that the government should leave the provision of consumer goods to private enterprise even as it encourages businesses to invest in certain locations, regulates their activities and helps low-income shoppers through various food assistance programs.

The reality is more complicated. For at least a century, New York’s food economy has not operated independently of government. In fact, public policies and investments have long shaped where supermarkets open, which businesses can operate with a profit, and how residents obtain food.
It’s just that they have done so in ways consumers often don’t see.

That is why the five grocery stores carry a broader significance, in my view. They offer a different model of public investment that makes the government much more visible in providing an essential service – and more accountable for its results. New Yorkers will get an opportunity to judge that contribution directly.
If the stores succeed, they may change not just what people expect to pay for groceries, but what they expect their city government to provide.
New York City has committed US$70 million to develop these stores, which will be open to all.
While they will be managed by private operators, the city will provide rent-free space, prioritize publicly owned sites and ensure that essential foods are priced 30% below typical retail prices.
In this respect, the stores offer a “public option” – a government-provided good or service that exists alongside private alternatives, like public schools and city hospitals.

Municipal grocery stores would offer New Yorkers a similar choice alongside private retailers. But as a public option, they would create a visible alternative against which shoppers can judge privately owned stores, setting a benchmark for food prices and service quality. They would also demonstrate how public investment can be used to make an essential good more affordable.
At his May announcement, Mamdani described the proposed Bronx store and its surrounding development as “physical proof of our conviction that government can be a force for good.”
A fresh form of intervention
Government-supported food retailing has a long history in New York City despite opposition by existing businesses.

In 1934, Mayor Fiorello La Guardia’s administration began selling discounted milk to low-income families, but the initiative drew complaints from grocers about unfair competition. Independent merchants similarly protested the city’s efforts to subsidize a new Pathmark supermarket in East Harlem in the 1990s, warning that it would put local grocers out of business.

A more recent example is the city’s Food Retail Expansion to Support Health program, known as FRESH. Since 2009, it has offered supermarket developers and operators long-term tax breaks and zoning incentives to build or expand dozens of stores in underserved neighborhoods.
These incentives have helped increase grocery retail space, but shoppers don’t see the public support behind them.

FRESH is just one example of an approach toward supermarket financing that gained momentum in the 1990s, when governments sought to address social problems by encouraging private investment. Food insecurity was blamed on a scarcity of neighborhood supermarkets, not on prices being beyond reach for local shoppers.

Subsidizing new stores promised better nutrition and economic development without confronting poverty or inequality, and FRESH reflects that approach. Participating supermarkets must devote space to perishable foods, but they’re not required to offer affordable prices. That may be one reason why researchers have found that adding supermarkets to low-income neighborhoods, by itself, doesn’t substantially improve residents’ diets.

This hidden government role is hardly confined to grocery stores. Much of what government does for Americans is delivered indirectly, through tax credits, subsidies and private institutions. Because the public contribution is obscured, people often give credit to private markets for the benefits provided by public policy, from student loans to healthcare.
This invisibility is a consequence of policy design and influences how citizens understand government, a phenomenon that political scientist Suzanne Mettler described as “the submerged state.”
Bringing the state into the open
Municipal grocery stores depart from the traditional model in two important ways.

First, they make affordability an explicit condition of public investment rather than the outcome of increased retail competition. Second, they make government’s contribution visible. For example, the stores will share distinct branding so shoppers know who’s responsible for the affordable food.

If the stores deliver reliable savings, shoppers may begin to see affordable food as something government can help provide, not an outcome determined entirely by private markets. When public benefits are obscured, people are more likely to underestimate government’s contribution to their lives. Visible programs, like a physical store in the neighborhood, make that contribution easier to notice and evaluate.

Visibility also creates accountability. A customer at a private supermarket that received a tax break to expand isn’t likely to tie the store’s prices or food quality to government policy. At a municipal grocery store, with clear branding, the connection is unmistakable.

To be sure, critics’ concerns deserve serious attention. Many independent grocery stores are owned by immigrant entrepreneurs operating on thin margins. Groups representing bodegas and independent supermarkets warn that a publicly subsidized competitor could draw away their customers. Some may lose business.

Yet East Harlem’s Pathmark demonstrates that new supermarkets and smaller retailers can coexist. Between 2000 and 2015, the number of small grocery stores and bodegas in the neighborhood increased from 100 to 126, while supermarkets rose from 10 to 18. That said, those figures don’t establish Pathmark’s effects on individual businesses.

The municipal stores’ impact on nearby retailers remains an open question. But the task for New York City is to ensure that private operators deliver excellent service and real savings, and that their commercial interests don’t undermine the public mission. It will also need to provide good working conditions and track effects on nearby businesses.
Ultimately, public ownership doesn’t guarantee success. But it makes government’s responsibility for the outcome impossible to miss.
Nevin Cohen receives research funding from the City of New York.

articles.title: Republican gerrymandering worked pretty well in Texas and Florida, even if it backfired in North Carolina and Ohio
articles.author: Charlie Hunt, Associate Professor of Political Science, Boise State University
paras: During the 2026 election cycle, Republicans enacted a series of gerrymanders – a form of partisan redistricting – in a handful of states to give them a disproportionate edge over Democrats in their congressional delegations. Democrats responded with a successful redistricting effort in California and an unsuccessful one in Virginia.
Gerrymandering has obvious implications for fairness and democracy, characterized by some as politicians picking their voters, not voters picking their politicians.
There’s also a practical consideration for those doing the gerrymandering: The efforts can fail when they overplay their hand.

By spreading their supportive voters across many districts, parties can create more seats that may lean in their direction. But if spread too thin, these efforts can backfire and net seats for the other party, particularly in a “wave” election year that favors the other party. This unintended consequence is often referred to as a “dummymander.”
So, with such massive Democratic majorities poised to enter the 120th Congress, did Republican attempts to gerrymander actually end up costing them some seats in the U.S. House?
The answer isn’t as clear-cut as you might think.
Dummymanders in North Carolina and Ohio?

Republican state legislatures in Ohio and North Carolina redrew their congressional maps in 2025, crafting a set of districts they believed would maximize the number of seats they could win in the House.

Despite both states being traditionally competitive in statewide elections, their state legislatures drew a collection of seats Republicans believed they would win: 12 of these 15 new seats in Ohio and 11 out of 14 in North Carolina included a majority of voters who voted for Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election.

But in 2026, Democrats across the country won dozens of seats that had previously seemed out of reach, including districts Trump won by double digits in 2024. Many of these seats were in heavily gerrymandered Republican seats.

In Ohio and North Carolina, the size and scope of the midterm backlash against Trump and his party put many of the seats Republicans targeted in these states, including ones Trump won by as many as 20 points, in serious jeopardy.
In the end, the Democratic wave overcame so many Trump-won seats in these states that their new delegations to Congress may be more Democratic than they would have been without the gerrymanders.
Democrats held the line in the deep South

Texas and Florida also targeted a series of Democrat-held seats to flip their way in 2026. Nine such seats across these two states, as well as a vulnerable seat held by Democratic U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures in Alabama, were the targets of gerrymanders that created new districts that Trump won in 2024, all by 9 percentage points or more.

But once the 2026 Democratic wave swept through the deep South, these gerrymanders were essentially canceled out. Despite the gains the party projected, Republicans in these three states appear likely to enter the 120th Congress with delegations the same size as they had in the 119th.

Other Republican gerrymandering attempts were successful, but only barely. In Tennessee’s 9th District, the last remaining Democratic seat in the state was gerrymandered into a district Donald Trump won by 21 points in 2024. Republicans did hold that seat as expected, but only by 2,500 votes, or just over 1 percentage point.
Gerrymanders that worked – and didn’t
Many of these gerrymanders were not maximally successful. But were they true dummymanders?
In North Carolina and Ohio it does appear that Republicans overplayed their hand by counting on past Trump voters in a national environment that proved so favorable to the Democrats.

In Ohio, a gerrymander that aimed for a two-thirds Republican majority in their House delegation will net them less than half of that in the 120th Congress. That outcome ended up producing a more representative result, one that was roughly in line with the two parties’ 2026 popular vote shares in the state.

North Carolina was a more drastic dummymander: The Republicans aimed to design districts where they would win seats accounting for almost two-thirds of their congressional delegation. But the party is currently poised to hold, at best, less than one-third of their state’s seats.

And California, which Democrats gerrymandered in reaction to Republican efforts in other states, is a partisan success story. The state is projected to send only 8% of their delegation to the House as Republicans, despite voting 30% for Republicans statewide.

In Texas and Florida the story is more complicated. Democrats in those states retained most of the seats they held that their Republican legislatures targeted in their gerrymanders, thanks to historic shifts by Hispanic voters who had voted for Trump in the 2024 election.

But gerrymanders can be effective beyond marginal, targeted districts. Taken as a whole, Texas’ and Florida’s district boundaries were drawn so favorably for Republicans that even a Democratic tsunami managed only to keep these states’ delegations identical in the next Congress, since many other districts remained safe for Republicans.

In these states, Republicans still enjoy a greater proportion of House seats than their popular vote margins would reflect. And in a less Democrat-leaning election cycle, many of these gerrymandered seats could very well shift back toward Republicans.
Failed GOP gerrymanders would have produced an even bigger blue wave

As poor as the outcome of the 2026 midterms was for Republicans, it could have been even worse. In fact, some Republican states might count themselves lucky that their attempts to gerrymander failed in the lead-up to the midterms.

In traditionally Republican states such as Missouri and Utah, courts struck down gerrymanders that would have created a series of districts that Trump won by around 20 percentage points. If the gerrymanders had not been struck down, Democrats’ shocking success in similar districts across the country could have netted them as many as five additional seats in these states.

A similar situation played out in Indiana and South Carolina. New maps pushed by Trump that failed in their state legislatures were intended to produce even more lopsided Republican gains. But analysis from the Cook Political Report found that these maps might have netted Democrats as many as six out of South Carolina’s seven House seats, and eight out of Indiana’s nine. Instead, Democrats seem likely to end up with only a pair of seats in each state.
What’s next in gerrymandering wars?
The 2026 election cycle demonstrates that gerrymandering is a far more complex and dynamic proposition than it is often treated by pundits and parties.

Wave elections of this size can often overcome the intended effects of gerrymandered maps, but subsequent elections might find them much more effective. Plus, parties often draw gerrymandered maps based on the previous election’s presidential results – a measure that may be less reliable as voters continue to make more unexpected choices.

Moreover, both red and blue states are dealing with the aftermath of the Louisiana v. Callais Supreme Court decision, which made the gerrymandering of racial groups easier to do without court interventions. Over the next two years, Republicans may attempt to implement even more new maps in many new states, particularly in the South. Those new districts will likely aim to dilute majority-Black districts that are no longer protected by the Voting Rights Act.
Meanwhile, Democratic state governments appear poised to continue with their pushback against last cycle’s Republican efforts with gerrymanders of their own over the next two years.
But the Republican redistricting failures of the 2026 cycle, including their near misses, should make both parties cautious about future attempts.
